card_obj.Text: Unlike their prokaryotic counterparts, eukaryotic RNA polymerases {{c1::cannot::can or cannot}} initiate transcription by themselves.
card_obj.Back Extra:
Why: all five eukaryotic RNA polymerases need protein transcription factors, which must bind the promoter and form an initiation complex before the polymerase itself will bind and start the RNA chain.

Distinguish: a prokaryotic RNA polymerase manages initiation itself because its sigma subunit recognizes the promoter and binds the enzyme to it; a eukaryotic polymerase has to wait for separate transcription factors to do that job.

Pitfall: basal transcription factors are required for initiation to happen at all; enhancers and silencers, with still other transcription factors, only modulate how efficiently a promoter initiates.

card_obj.Text: A spliceosome is in many ways like a small {{c1::ribosome::comparable particle}}: an RNA–protein machine that contains a set of small RNAs called {{c2::snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs)::its RNA class}} together with about {{c3::40::how many}} different proteins.
card_obj.Back Extra:
Why: like a ribosome, the spliceosome is a ribonucleoprotein whose RNA parts do recognition work — the 5′ splice site is read by base-pairing with U1 snRNA.

Pitfall: 40 is the protein count of the whole spliceosome; each individual snRNP carries a subset of seven common snRNP proteins plus one or more of its own.
